screens.title: Network Configuration and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build practical skills for configuring network interfaces and diagnosing connectivity on Linux systems. We'll cover the two common ways a machine gets an IP address — dynamic assignment with DHCP and manually set static addresses — and show how to use modern command-line tools like ip and nmcli to make changes that take effect immediately. You will also learn how DNS fits into the picture and how to validate name resolution with dig. The goal is not just to run commands but to understand what each step verifies: link state, assigned address and mask, routing table, gateway reachability, and DNS servers. Consider which approach your distribution prefers and why a static address matters for production services.

screens.title: Using ip for immediate interface changes
screens.narratorSegment: The ip command is the modern, distribution-agnostic tool for inspecting and temporarily modifying network interfaces and routes. When you need to test an IP assignment or bring a link up without changing persistent files, ip is the safest instrument. For example, assigning 192.168.1.100 with a 24-bit mask to eth0 is done with ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev eth0, followed by ip link set eth0 up to activate the link. These changes modify the kernel state immediately but are lost after reboot or a service restart. Use ip a (short for ip addr show) to confirm the address is present and ip r (ip route show) to ensure the default route points to the correct gateway. A common misconception is that running ip commands edits config files; it does not. If you want permanence, you must edit distribution-specific files or use tools like nmcli. Another pitfall is assigning an IP in the wrong network: if the gateway is in a different subnet, packets will never reach it. To illustrate, after adding the address and bringing the interface up, test connectivity by pinging the gateway and an external IP such as 8.8.8.8. If the gateway ping fails, double-check link state, cable or virtual network connection, and the assigned subnet. Practice this temporary workflow when you want a quick verification without making persistent changes. How would you test a new address without disturbing services?

keyIdea.text: ip modifies kernel network state immediately but not persistent configs. Use ip for quick tests; use config files or nmcli for persistence.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Using ip
ip: immediate interface changes
Assign an address and bring a link up for testing without editing files.
Example commands
sudo ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev eth0
sudo ip link set eth0 up
sudo ip route add default via 192.168.1.1

# Verify
ip a show eth0
ip r show
These commands update the kernel tables. Remember: they are temporary and ideal for checks or troubleshooting before making persistent changes.
Explanation and checklist
  • Bringing the link up activates the interface; without it, the address won't be used.
  • Default route points outbound traffic to the gateway — confirm with ip r.
  • Temporary change does not edit /etc files; to persist, update distro config or nmcli.
  • Common mistake: mismatched subnet and gateway prevents external access even when an IP is assigned.
Concrete check
Key Takeaway

Use ip to make immediate changes and validate with ping before applying persistent configuration.

screens.title: Persisting configuration: distro files and nmcli
screens.narratorSegment: Temporary ip edits are useful for immediate testing, but production systems require persistent configuration. Different distributions and services use distinct files. On Debian-based systems you commonly edit /etc/network/interfaces with an iface stanza specifying address, netmask, gateway, and dns-nameservers. On Red Hat-based systems, an ifcfg-eth0 file in /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts holds variables like BOOTPROTO, IPADDR, NETMASK, and GATEWAY. Many modern systems prefer NetworkManager; its nmcli CLI lets you modify a connection object and bring it up. For example, nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.150/24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" ipv4. method manual followed by nmcli connection up eth0 applies the persistent change managed by NetworkManager. A common misconception is that all distros use the same config file — they do not. Another pitfall is editing /etc/resolv. conf directly when it is managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager, leading to overwritten changes. When editing files, remember to restart the appropriate network service or bring interfaces down and up to apply settings. In environments with configuration management, persistent files may be templated by higher-level tools, so coordinate changes accordingly. Which persistent method maps to your server images?

keyIdea.title: Persistence matters
keyIdea.text: Distribution and service determine where persistent network settings live. Use nmcli for NetworkManager-managed systems and edit distro files only when appropriate.

content.html:
Persistent configuration
Edit the correct file or use nmcli so settings survive reboots and service restarts.
Debian-style example
auto eth0
iface eth0 inet static
    address 192.168.1.100
    netmask 255.255.255.0
    gateway 192.168.1.1
    dns-nameservers 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4
After editing: sudo systemctl restart networking or bring interface down/up.
Red Hat-style example
TYPE=Ethernet
BOOTPROTO=static
NAME=eth0
DEVICE=eth0
ONBOOT=yes
IPADDR=192.168.1.100
NETMASK=255.255.255.0
GATEWAY=192.168.1.1
DNS1=8.8.8.8
DNS2=8.8.4.4
Restart NetworkManager: sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager
nmcli persistent change
sudo nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.150/24 \
  ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" ipv4.method manual
sudo nmcli connection up eth0
If NetworkManager controls the interface, prefer nmcli. Editing files when NM is active can create conflicts.

screens.title: DHCP vs Static IP addresses
screens.narratorSegment: DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, automates IP addressing so clients receive an address, netmask, default gateway, and DNS servers from a central server. It is ideal for desktop machines and ephemeral instances where manual management would be error-prone. A static IP is a manual, fixed address configured on the host; it ensures predictable reachability and is commonly used for servers, DNS hosts, routers, and any service that must be reached at a known address. A useful rule of thumb: use DHCP for general-purpose clients and static where other systems must reliably connect to the host. A frequent misconception is that DHCP cannot be used for servers at all; in fact, DHCP reservations can provide fixed addressing while keeping central management, but many administrators prefer explicit static configuration for critical infrastructure. When choosing an approach, consider your operational practices — does your environment use centralized address management and DHCP reservations, or do you require immutable addresses in configuration management? Also think about DNS: a static server often pairs with a manual DNS record to ensure permanence. Finally, remember that switching modes changes resolver and route behavior and may require restarting services. Reflect on your infrastructure: which approach reduces risk for your services?

keyIdea.text: DHCP is convenient and centrally managed; static addresses provide predictable reachability for services. Use reservations for a middle ground when available.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › DHCP vs Static
DHCP versus Static IP
Understand the operational trade-offs and when each method is appropriate.
DHCP (dynamic)
Automates assignment from a central server. Good for clients and large fleets where manual changes would be slow. Supports leases and reservations for predictability.
Misconception: DHCP always changes addresses. In many setups, reservations make addresses effectively fixed.
Static (manual)
Manually set on the host or via configuration management. Preferred for servers and infrastructure requiring a stable address that external systems use.
Pitfall: forgetting to update DNS records when assigning a static address can make the service unreachable by name.
Concrete example
A lab workstation can use DHCP for portability. A database server hosting production data should use a static IP so application configs and DNS records reliably reference it.
Key Takeaway

Match addressing strategy to operational needs: convenience for clients, predictability for services.

screens.title: Troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: Effective troubleshooting starts with a fixed, repeatable sequence so you can narrow the fault quickly. Begin with physical and link-level checks: ensure cables or virtual NICs are present and link lights or VM console indicate the interface is up. Next, validate the network stack locally: ping 127.0.0.1 tests kernel network functionality and ping your assigned IP to confirm the interface responds. Then check the interface state and IP assignment with ip a and confirm the routing table with ip r — is the default route present and correct? The next step is gateway reachability: ping your gateway IP; failure here points to local network or gateway misconfiguration. If the gateway is reachable, test external connectivity by pinging a public IP like 8.8.8.8 — if that succeeds but pinging a hostname fails, you have a DNS problem. Use dig to query a hostname and identify which resolver answered. Also inspect open ports and listening services using ss -tuln to ensure services are actually available on expected ports. Finally, check firewall rules; ufw status or firewall-cmd --list-all can reveal blocked traffic. A common error is restarting NetworkManager on a production host without warning; always consider impact before disruptive steps. Following this ordered checklist reduces guesswork and helps you document each change. What would your first step be for a production web server that suddenly becomes unreachable?

keyIdea.text: Follow a fixed order: link check → loopback → assigned IP → gateway → external IP → hostname/DNS → firewall/services. This narrows scope quickly.

content.html:
Troubleshooting checklist
Work outward from the host to the network and DNS.
Step 1
Physical / Link
Check cable or VM NIC and link state.
Step 2
Loopback & Interface
ping 127.0.0.1, ping assigned IP, ip a show
Step 3
Routing
ip r show — confirm default route to gateway
Step 4
Gateway
ping 192.168.1.1 — failure indicates local network issue
Step 5
External IP
ping 8.8.8.8 — tests Internet reachability without DNS
Step 6
Hostname / DNS
ping google.com; if failing, run dig to inspect resolver
Common mistake
Restarting NetworkManager or the network service without scheduling can disrupt users and hide intermittent problems. Always document and, when possible, perform disruptive commands during a maintenance window.
Pro tip

When in doubt, run simple non-destructive checks first: ip a, ip r, ping gateway, ping public IP. These reveal scope quickly.

screens.title: Reading and diagnosing DNS issues
screens.narratorSegment: A common symptom is that a service is reachable by IP but not by hostname. This points to a DNS resolution issue. To diagnose, first confirm that pinging an external IP, such as 8.8.8.8, succeeds — that ensures routing and gateway reachability. Next, run dig for the troubled hostname; dig reveals which DNS server was queried, the response, and any errors. Inspect /etc/resolv. conf to see configured resolvers, but be cautious: files managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager may overwrite manual edits. Another useful command is getent hosts hostname which consults configured name service switch settings. A frequent misconception is that DNS failures are always caused by remote servers; often the local resolver list is wrong or a firewall blocks DNS (UDP/TCP port 53). If dig returns no answer, try dig @8.8.8.8 hostname to test using a known public resolver — success here indicates your local resolver chain is at fault. Finally, ensure your network's DNS settings are applied via DHCP or persistent configs so clients receive correct resolvers. When debugging, ask: is the DNS chain broken locally or upstream? Reading and diagnosing DNS issues means if ip works but hostname doesn't, test external ip first, then use dig to identify which resolver fails. check local resolver settings in /etc/resolv.conf and resolver services.. In practical terms, when hostname resolution fails but direct ip works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Diagnosing DNS failures
Isolate whether DNS is the cause when IP connectivity exists but hostnames fail.
Workflow
  1. ping a known IP (8.8.8.8) to confirm routing.
  2. Use dig hostname to see resolver response and which server answered.
  3. Inspect /etc/resolv.conf for configured nameservers, noting any manager that could overwrite it.
  4. Try dig @8.8.8.8 hostname to test an external resolver.
Example command
dig google.com
# If that fails:
dig @8.8.8.8 google.com
cat /etc/resolv.conf
If dig @8.8.8.8 works, your resolver chain is at fault; edit NetworkManager or DHCP settings instead of /etc/resolv.conf directly when managed services are present.
Key Takeaway

IP connectivity plus hostname failure equals DNS. Use dig and a known public resolver to separate local resolver issues from upstream DNS problems.

screens.title: Practical nmcli demo: set static on eth0
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a practical nmcli scenario to convert an eth0 connection from DHCP to static addressing. This is common on systems managed by NetworkManager. The sequence is: modify the connection object, apply it, and then verify addresses, routes, and DNS. The commands shown are precisely those you will run: first modify with nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.150/24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" ipv4. method manual, then bring the connection up with nmcli connection up eth0. After applying the change verify with ip a show eth0 to confirm the address, ip r show to see the default via the gateway, and cat /etc/resolv. conf to ensure DNS entries are present. A common misconception is that nmcli changes are immediate but not persistent; in reality, nmcli modifies NetworkManager's connection profile persistently unless you explicitly use a volatile flag. If your system doesn't use NetworkManager, nmcli may not have effect and you should edit distro files instead. When running nmcli connection up, be mindful that it can briefly disrupt connectivity while re-establishing the link. Use this workflow during maintenance windows on production hosts or perform in a console with a separate access path.

When running nmcli connection up, be mindful that it can briefly disrupt connectivity while re-establishing the link. Use this workflow during maintenance windows on production hosts or perform in a console with a separate access path.

keyIdea.title: nmcli workflow
keyIdea.text: nmcli modifies NetworkManager profiles persistently. After changes, verify with ip a, ip r, and checking resolv.conf to confirm DNS resolution settings.

content.html:
nmcli demo: set static IP
Modify the connection profile and verify system state with ip and resolv.conf.
Run these commands
sudo nmcli connection modify eth0 \
  ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.150/24 \
  ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" \
  ipv4.method manual

sudo nmcli connection up eth0
nmcli edits the profile stored by NetworkManager and then brings the connection up using the new settings.
Verify results
ip a show eth0
ip r show
cat /etc/resolv.conf
If resolv.conf is managed by systemd-resolved, the contents may point to a local resolver; use systemd-resolve --status or nmcli to inspect the applied DNS.
Key Takeaway

nmcli is the right tool when NetworkManager controls interfaces; verify address, route, and DNS after applying changes and avoid disruptive restarts on production systems.

screens.title: Verify routing and sockets
screens.narratorSegment: After assigning addresses and ensuring link state, confirm that the system will forward packets correctly and that services are listening where expected. Use ip route show to inspect the routing table; the default route, often listed as default via 192.168.1.1, determines how packets reach external networks. If the default route is missing or incorrect, external connectivity will fail even with a correct local IP. The ss command replaces older netstat for viewing sockets: ss -tuln shows TCP and UDP sockets that are listening with numeric addresses. This helps you confirm whether a web server is bound to the expected interface and port. A common misconception is assuming a service is reachable because the process is running; if the service listens only on localhost, remote connections will fail. Use ss to verify the bind address. Also inspect firewall rules; a listening service behind an active firewall could still be unreachable. For example, ss -tuln might show that nginx is listening on 127.0.0.1:80 — this indicates a configuration issue in the service, not the network. Combine ip r and ss outputs when diagnosing reachability problems and update service or firewall settings accordingly. How would you tell if a service is listening only locally?

keyIdea.text: Confirm default route for outbound traffic and use ss to ensure services bind to the correct addresses; local-only binds cause remote connection failures even with network access.

content.html:
Routing and socket checks
Use ip and ss to verify outbound path and service bindings.
Check routing
ip route show
# Expect a default route like:
# default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto static metric 100
No default route means no outbound connectivity. Add a default route with ip route add default via if needed.
Check listening sockets
ss -tuln
# Look for lines like:
# LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:80 0.0.0.0:*
# or 127.0.0.1:80 which is localhost-only
If a service binds to 127.0.0.1 only, edit its config to bind to 0.0.0.0 or the specific interface IP for external access.
Common mistake

Assuming services are reachable because they run. Always verify listen address with ss and routing with ip to find the true cause of unreachable services.

screens.title: Applied scenario: convert DHCP to static and verify
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on scenario walks you through changing an eth0 interface from DHCP to a chosen static configuration and then verifying connectivity. Start by recording current state: ip a show eth0, ip route show, and cat /etc/resolv. conf. Choose a static address such as 192.168.1.150/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS servers 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4. Use nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.150/24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" ipv4. method manual, then nmcli connection up eth0 to apply. After applying, verify ip a shows the new address and ip r shows default via the expected gateway. Check DNS with cat /etc/resolv. conf and run ping -c 4 192.168.1.1 to test gateway reachability. Then ping -c 4 8.8.8.8 to confirm external IP reachability. If external IP succeeds but ping google. com fails, use dig google. com to check DNS and dig @8.8.8.8 google. com to verify an external resolver. If anything fails, reverse the change or reconfigure per your distro's files. Remember to notify users before restarting network services on production systems. This scenario is deliberately conservative: apply changes, verify each layer, and only then trust the persistent configuration. Which verification step gave you the most confidence that connectivity was restored?

content.html:
Lab: DHCP → Static on eth0
Follow these commands and checks exactly as shown to avoid unintended downtime.
Record current state
ip a show eth0
ip route show
cat /etc/resolv.conf
Keep this output to revert or to compare after changes.
Apply persistent static (nmcli)
sudo nmcli connection modify eth0 \
  ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.150/24 \
  ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \
  ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" \

ip route show             # default route via gateway

Apply changes conservatively and verify each layer before declaring success. Keep rollback notes for production systems.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build practical skills for configuring network interfaces and diagnosing connectivity on Linux systems. We'll cover the two common ways a machine gets an IP address — dynamic assignment with DHCP and manually set static addresses — and show how to use modern command-line tools like ip and nmcli to make changes that take effect immediately. You will also learn how DNS fits into the picture and how to validate name resolution with dig. The goal is not just to run commands but to understand what each step verifies: link state, assigned address and mask, routing table, gateway reachability, and DNS servers. We'll walk through a hands-on scenario that changes an interface from DHCP to a static address, then validate connectivity from loopback to external hostname lookups. Along the way you'll see common mistakes, such as forgetting to restart network services or misconfiguring the gateway, and how those errors appear in tests like ping and dig. By the end you will be able to choose the correct configuration approach for servers or clients, apply a static address safely, and follow a repeatable troubleshooting checklist to restore connectivity. Consider which approach your distribution prefers and why a static address matters for production services.

By the end of this chapter you will confidently configure network interfaces, decide between DHCP and static addressing, and use standard Linux utilities to verify connectivity and name resolution. First, you'll learn to apply a temporary configuration with ip for quick tests and a persistent change using distribution files or nmcli. Next, you'll distinguish when DHCP's convenience is acceptable and when servers require static addresses; you'll see how routing and gateway settings control external access. Third, you'll practice essential diagnostics using ping, traceroute, ss or netstat, and dig to pinpoint whether problems are physical, routing-related, or DNS-based. Finally, you'll adopt a safe troubleshooting checklist that starts from loopback and moves outward, minimizing risky changes on production hosts. Each objective pairs a command-level skill with an explanation of why it matters — for example, using dig shows which DNS server answered a query so you can correct resolver settings. These measurable outcomes let you verify your competency through hands-on steps and short troubleshooting scenarios. Which of these objectives feels most relevant to your current environment?

This lesson follows a mixed-format flow to build both conceptual understanding and practical muscle memory. First, a three-minute slide section explains DHCP versus static addressing, where distribution-specific configuration files live, and why you would choose one method over the other. That gives the conceptual shape you need. Second, a seven-minute terminal demonstration uses nmcli and ip to change an eth0 interface from DHCP to a static address, verify the interface and routing table, and show how resolv. conf reflects DNS settings. The demo includes real verification commands so you can read outputs and recognize correct states. Third, we run a stepwise troubleshooting sequence: loopback checks, interface and IP verification, gateway pings, external IP versus hostname tests, and DNS queries with dig. We also cover reading ss or netstat to confirm listening services. Finally, you'll be prompted to reflect on your distribution's preferred configuration method and how restarting services can temporarily disrupt production traffic. This structure helps you move from knowledge to confident practice.

The ip command is the modern, distribution-agnostic tool for inspecting and temporarily modifying network interfaces and routes. When you need to test an IP assignment or bring a link up without changing persistent files, ip is the safest instrument. For example, assigning 192.168.1.100 with a 24-bit mask to eth0 is done with ip addr add 192.168.1.100/24 dev eth0, followed by ip link set eth0 up to activate the link. These changes modify the kernel state immediately but are lost after reboot or a service restart. Use ip a (short for ip addr show) to confirm the address is present and ip r (ip route show) to ensure the default route points to the correct gateway. A common misconception is that running ip commands edits config files; it does not. If you want permanence, you must edit distribution-specific files or use tools like nmcli. Another pitfall is assigning an IP in the wrong network: if the gateway is in a different subnet, packets will never reach it. To illustrate, after adding the address and bringing the interface up, test connectivity by pinging the gateway and an external IP such as 8.8.8.8. If the gateway ping fails, double-check link state, cable or virtual network connection, and the assigned subnet. Practice this temporary workflow when you want a quick verification without making persistent changes. How would you test a new address without disturbing services?

Temporary ip edits are useful for immediate testing, but production systems require persistent configuration. Different distributions and services use distinct files. On Debian-based systems you commonly edit /etc/network/interfaces with an iface stanza specifying address, netmask, gateway, and dns-nameservers. On Red Hat-based systems, an ifcfg-eth0 file in /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts holds variables like BOOTPROTO, IPADDR, NETMASK, and GATEWAY. Many modern systems prefer NetworkManager; its nmcli CLI lets you modify a connection object and bring it up. For example, nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv4. addresses 192.168.1.150/24 ipv4. gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4. dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4" ipv4. method manual followed by nmcli connection up eth0 applies the persistent change managed by NetworkManager. A common misconception is that all distros use the same config file — they do not. Another pitfall is editing /etc/resolv. conf directly when it is managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager, leading to overwritten changes. When editing files, remember to restart the appropriate network service or bring interfaces down and up to apply settings. In environments with configuration management, persistent files may be templated by higher-level tools, so coordinate changes accordingly. Which persistent method maps to your server images?

DHCP, the Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, automates IP addressing so clients receive an address, netmask, default gateway, and DNS servers from a central server. It is ideal for desktop machines and ephemeral instances where manual management would be error-prone. A static IP is a manual, fixed address configured on the host; it ensures predictable reachability and is commonly used for servers, DNS hosts, routers, and any service that must be reached at a known address. A useful rule of thumb: use DHCP for general-purpose clients and static where other systems must reliably connect to the host. A frequent misconception is that DHCP cannot be used for servers at all; in fact, DHCP reservations can provide fixed addressing while keeping central management, but many administrators prefer explicit static configuration for critical infrastructure. When choosing an approach, consider your operational practices — does your environment use centralized address management and DHCP reservations, or do you require immutable addresses in configuration management? Also think about DNS: a static server often pairs with a manual DNS record to ensure permanence. Finally, remember that switching modes changes resolver and route behavior and may require restarting services. Reflect on your infrastructure: which approach reduces risk for your services?

Effective troubleshooting starts with a fixed, repeatable sequence so you can narrow the fault quickly. Begin with physical and link-level checks: ensure cables or virtual NICs are present and link lights or VM console indicate the interface is up. Next, validate the network stack locally: ping 127.0.0.1 tests kernel network functionality and ping your assigned IP to confirm the interface responds. Then check the interface state and IP assignment with ip a and confirm the routing table with ip r — is the default route present and correct? The next step is gateway reachability: ping your gateway IP; failure here points to local network or gateway misconfiguration. If the gateway is reachable, test external connectivity by pinging a public IP like 8.8.8.8 — if that succeeds but pinging a hostname fails, you have a DNS problem. Use dig to query a hostname and identify which resolver answered. Also inspect open ports and listening services using ss -tuln to ensure services are actually available on expected ports. Finally, check firewall rules; ufw status or firewall-cmd --list-all can reveal blocked traffic. A common error is restarting NetworkManager on a production host without warning; always consider impact before disruptive steps. Following this ordered checklist reduces guesswork and helps you document each change. What would your first step be for a production web server that suddenly becomes unreachable?

A common symptom is that a service is reachable by IP but not by hostname. This points to a DNS resolution issue. To diagnose, first confirm that pinging an external IP, such as 8.8.8.8, succeeds — that ensures routing and gateway reachability. Next, run dig for the troubled hostname; dig reveals which DNS server was queried, the response, and any errors. Inspect /etc/resolv. conf to see configured resolvers, but be cautious: files managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager may overwrite manual edits. Another useful command is getent hosts hostname which consults configured name service switch settings. A frequent misconception is that DNS failures are always caused by remote servers; often the local resolver list is wrong or a firewall blocks DNS (UDP/TCP port 53). If dig returns no answer, try dig @8.8.8.8 hostname to test using a known public resolver — success here indicates your local resolver chain is at fault. Finally, ensure your network's DNS settings are applied via DHCP or persistent configs so clients receive correct resolvers. When debugging, ask: is the DNS chain broken locally or upstream?
